judge_assessment.explanation: The mathematics is exactly as the judge describes and I re-derived all of it: problem 1's sin(theta)(2cos(theta)-1) = 0 giving 0, 60, 180, 300; problem 3's cos(theta)(2cos(theta)-1) = 0 giving 60, 90, 270, 300 with 90 and 270 as the branch Nils divided away; problem 5's difference-of-squares route avoiding the square root entirely; problem 6's four candidates reduced to 90 and 180 by substitution, with the rejected pair shown to satisfy sin - cos = -1; and problem 7's double-angle reduction to (2cos+1)(cos-1) = 0 giving 0, 120, 240. The numerical counter-tests are right too: 1.5 against Bea's 0.5, and 2.5 against the student's 1.75. The judge is also right that the key states the domain qualification on the cancelled factor ('valid for cos x != 1'), which is the detail most keys drop. Two things the judge did not weigh. First, the worksheet's own directions say 'In each problem: name the error in words first, then show corrected work', and each of problems 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7 opens with a written diagnosis sub-part — 'Name what Rafi's division assumed without saying so', 'Explain why the cos x in the numerator cannot be cancelled', 'Say what taking a square root leaves out', 'Say what squaring did to the problem', 'Explain why equal cosine values do not force equal angles'. Every one of those problems is recorded in verify.json as a single machine entry with no manual companion; only problem 8 is manual, and the judge accordingly reviewed one open item when the sheet prints six. On a misconception-analysis worksheet the named diagnosis IS the assessed skill, so this is the largest unverified surface on the sheet. Second, problems 3(a) and 7(b) explicitly ask the student to produce the factored form with zero on one side, and although that expression is literally present in verify.json as the solve_interval expr, it is never a declared expected, so the Quick Answers bank prints only the root lists ('3. 60, 90, 270, 300', '7. 0, 120, 240') and problem 3(b)'s 'say which ones Nils's division threw away' (90 and 270) is likewise uncovered. ACCEPT is still right — nothing here is wrong — but the perfect 32 overstates verification completeness.

strengths_to_preserve: The key supplies a reusable diagnostic, not just corrections: 'a solution set that is a strict subset of the true one is the signature of a division. Ask what was divided by and set it to zero', and in problem 3, 'the lost solutions are always the zeros of whatever you divided by'. That converts the whole topic into a two-step procedure a student can run on their own work.

Problem 6 is the one item that runs the opposite way — squaring ADDS solutions — and the key makes the contrast explicit in problem 6's teaching point ('dividing removes solutions, squaring adds them. Both are fixed by the same discipline') and again in problem 8(c). Putting the extraneous-root case inside a lost-solution sheet is what makes the distinction survive.

Problem 8(b)'s model answer carries a concrete arithmetic counterexample: (2+6)/2 = 4, but 'cancelling the 2' would give 6, and the legal move is 2/2 + 6/2 = 1 + 3 = 4. A numerical instance of the factor-versus-term rule is worth more than the rule stated again.

Problem 7's diagnosis is the sharpest on the sheet: 'cancelling the cosine treats cos as a multiplier, but it is a function, and it is not one-to-one on a full turn: cos 120 = cos 240 while 120 != 240.' The error is reclassified rather than merely corrected, and the counterexample is the same pair of angles the correct solution recovers.

final_response.md audits its own gate log honestly rather than claiming a clean sweep: it reports 31 of 34 prose numbers matched and explains each of the three flags, including that 270 degrees is one of Ola's EXTRANEOUS candidates and is therefore correctly absent from the verified solution set. It also states plainly which planted errors could not be declared as traps and why. That is the right posture for a delivery note.

The standard tags are genuinely looked up rather than approximated: references/standards-map.md line 100 carries 'Trig identities | HSF-TF.C.8' and line 99 'Trig functions & unit circle | HSF-TF.A.2, HSF-TF.B.5', matching the key's curriculum block exactly. No lower-grade substitution and no invented code.

root_causes.description: Six of the eight problems print a written-diagnosis sub-part and only one problem carries a manual entry. The worksheet's directions elevate the diagnosis to a requirement in every item ('name the error in words first'), and the instructional mode is misconception-analysis, where naming the error is the skill being taught. Recording problems 1, 4, 5, 6 and 7 as fully machine-verified therefore misstates what was checked on the majority of the sheet.
evidence: worksheet.pdf directions: 'In each problem: name the error in words first, then show corrected work.'

worksheet.pdf 1(a) 'Name what Rafi's division assumed without saying so'; 4(a) 'Explain why the cos x in the numerator cannot be cancelled against the denominator'; 5(a) 'Say what taking a square root leaves out'; 6(a) 'Say what squaring did to the problem'; 7(a) 'Explain why equal cosine values do not force equal angles'.
verify.json ids 1, 4, 5, 6, 7 each contain exactly one machine entry (solve_interval or eval) and no manual entry; only id 8 has type 'manual'.
answer_key.pdf answers each of those diagnosis parts in a 'Step 1: name the slip' paragraph, so the author wrote the expected response without declaring the slot.

root_causes.description: Two problems ask for a factored form as a distinct printed answer, and one asks which specific solutions the fictional student discarded. None of the three is a declared expected value, so the bank shows only the final root lists. The factored expressions are ironic near-misses: they already sit in verify.json as the solve_interval 'expr' strings, so the correct answer is in the data but is being used as an input rather than surfaced as an answer.
evidence: worksheet.pdf 3(a): 'Write the equation in factored form with 0 on one side.' verify.json id 3 expr is 'cos(theta)*(2*cos(theta) - 1)' but expected is the root list [60, 90, 270, 300].

worksheet.pdf 7(b): 'use a double-angle identity to write the equation with 0 on one side, factor it, and list every solution.' verify.json id 7 expr is '(2*cos(theta) + 1)*(cos(theta) - 1)', expected [0, 120, 240].
worksheet.pdf 3(b): 'say which ones Nils's division threw away' — the answer 90 and 270 is determinate and uncovered.
answer_key.pdf Quick Answers rows: '3. 60, 90, 270, 300' and '7. 0, 120, 240', with no factored form.

root_causes.description: The prompt required that planted wrong results be declared as machine-checked misconception traps, and five of the seven planted results could not be, because verify.py's _TRAP_TYPES excludes solve_interval — validate_traps raises 'type ... cannot carry traps — a trap needs a single comparable answer'. But the characteristic error of this entire topic produces a wrong SOLUTION SET, not a wrong scalar, so the trap mechanism is structurally unavailable exactly where the focus lives. The author worked around it by making every printed wrong angle one of the verified roots, which prevents drift but does not machine-check that the wrong set is a proper subset produced by the stated wrong method.
evidence: scripts/verify.py validate_traps: 'if ptype not in _TRAP_TYPES: raise VerifyInputError(f"type {ptype!r} cannot carry traps ...")', and the _TRAP_TYPES set does not include solve_interval.
Only verify.json ids 2 and 4 carry traps (the scalars 0.5 and 1.75); the five lost-solution items carry none.
final_response.md states the limitation explicitly: 'The traps field is scalar-only by design ... so those five could not be declared as traps.'
The task prompt: 'Declare any planted wrong results as machine-checked misconception traps.'

improvements.title: Require a manual entry for the named-diagnosis half of every find-and-fix item
improvements.proposed_change: Make the misconception-analysis mode carry a structural rule in SKILL.md and references/manual-review-aid.md: a find-and-fix item has two responses — the named error and the corrected work — and the named error is never machine-checkable, so each such problem needs a manual verify entry scoped to that sub-part in addition to its machine entries. Enforce it with a gate that fails when a worksheet whose directions or stems contain a diagnosis imperative ('name the error', 'name what ... assumed', 'say what ... leaves out', 'explain why ...') has verify ids for those problems with no manual component. render_quick_answers.py should then show a manual marker on those rows so the grader sees which half is theirs.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture reproducing curr-424 problem 1: stem containing 'Name what Rafi's division assumed without saying so' with a verify id whose only entry is a solve_interval. The gate must exit non-zero naming the unflagged diagnosis, and pass once a manual entry is added. Assert the reported manual-item count for a full curr-424-shaped fixture rises from 1 to 6.
improvements.expected_impact: On this sheet it corrects a five-fold understatement of the manual surface: the worksheet requires a written diagnosis in every find-and-fix item and declares one manual item. Across the misconception-analysis mode it is the difference between a package that reports what it checked and one that implies it checked the diagnosis.
improvements.risk: Under a machine_first review_mode this raises manual load, which the mode is designed to minimise. The right resolution is that the mode constrains what should be PRINTED, not what may be left unrecorded; that trade-off should be stated in SKILL.md or authors will be tempted to strip the diagnosis sub-parts, which would gut the instructional mode.

improvements.title: Surface the requested factored form as a declared answer instead of only using it as the solve_interval input
improvements.proposed_change: Add a response-slot inventory that binds each printed request to a declared expected value, and allow a solve_interval entry to carry an optional 'factored_form' expected that is checked for equivalence against the original equation and rendered in the bank alongside the roots. That is a small change with an outsized effect here, because the factored expression is already the entry's expr — the data exists and is simply not being reported as an answer. Also require an entry for derived sub-answers such as 'which solutions did the division throw away', which is computable as the set difference between the verified roots and the roots of the reduced equation.
improvements.regression_test: Fixture from curr-424 problem 3: prompt asks for the factored form with 0 on one side, for every solution, and for which solutions the division discarded; verify.json declares only solve_interval expr 'cos(theta)*(2*cos(theta) - 1)' expected [60, 90, 270, 300]. The gate must fail naming the two uncovered slots. After declaring the factored form and the lost-root set, the fixture passes and the bank row reads 'cos(theta)(2cos(theta) - 1) = 0; 60, 90, 270, 300; lost: 90, 270'.
improvements.expected_impact: Restores two requested answers per affected problem to the grading column and makes the lost-solution pair — the actual point of a lost-solution worksheet — an explicitly verified quantity rather than prose in the key.
improvements.risk: A factored form is not unique (sign and constant factors can be distributed differently), so the check must be equivalence-plus-shape rather than string equality, and the bank must print the author's literal string to avoid the sympify re-normalisation that damaged curr-404's factored answer.

improvements.title: Extend misconception traps to solution sets so a lost-solution error can be machine-declared
improvements.proposed_change: Add solve_interval (and any other set-valued type) to verify.py's _TRAP_TYPES with a set-aware trap shape: {"desc": ..., "expr": <the reduced equation the wrong method produces>, "value": [<the wrong solution list>]}. check_traps then verifies that the wrong method's root set is a PROPER SUBSET of the verified set (for a division/lost-solution error) or a proper superset (for a squaring/extraneous-root error), and that the printed wrong list matches it exactly. That is a stronger guarantee than the current workaround, which only ensures each printed wrong angle is some verified root and would not catch a planted wrong set that is missing the wrong angles.
improvements.regression_test: Declare on curr-424 problem 1 a trap {"desc": "divided by sin theta", "expr": "2*cos(theta) - 1", "value": [60, 300]} and assert verify.py accepts it, computes the reduced equation's roots as [60, 300], and confirms that set is a proper subset of [0, 60, 180, 300] with the difference [0, 180] reported. Today this raises VerifyInputError('type solve_interval cannot carry traps'). Add a negative case where the declared wrong list does not match the reduced equation's roots and assert it fails.
improvements.expected_impact: Makes the prompt's explicit requirement — 'declare any planted wrong results as machine-checked misconception traps' — satisfiable on the topic where the misconception is precisely a wrong solution set. Five of this sheet's seven planted errors become machine-checked instead of hand-bound, and the derived 'which solutions were lost' answer falls out of the same computation.
improvements.risk: Set comparison over trigonometric roots needs a tolerance and a canonical ordering, and a reduced equation can legitimately have roots outside the interval, so the subset check must be performed after interval filtering. Widening _TRAP_TYPES also risks authors declaring traps on types where 'distinguishably wrong' is ill-defined, so the new shape should be accepted only with an explicit relation field (subset or superset).

case_summary: The strongest sheet in this batch on instructional design. Seven find-and-fix items cover both halves of the focus — three division/lost-solution errors, two illegal-cancellation errors, one lost sign branch and one extraneous-root case that runs the opposite way — and the key gives a reusable diagnostic ('a strict subset of the true solution set is the signature of a division; the lost roots are the zeros of whatever you divided by') rather than only corrections. I verified every solution set, both numerical counter-tests and the standards tags against references/standards-map.md lines 99-100; all correct, and ACCEPT is right. Three verification gaps sit under the perfect 32. Six problems print a written-diagnosis sub-part and only problem 8 is declared manual, so the judge reviewed one open item on a sheet whose directions require naming the error in every problem. Problems 3(a) and 7(b) ask for a factored form that already exists in verify.json as the solve_interval expr but is never a declared expected, and 3(b)'s 'which solutions did the division throw away' is likewise uncovered. And verify.py's _TRAP_TYPES excludes solve_interval, so five of the seven planted wrong results could not be declared as traps at all — a limitation the author correctly diagnosed and documented in final_response.md rather than hiding, but one that leaves the prompt's trap requirement only partly met.
